title: Burgers, Lipstick & Underwear
subtitle: What Strange Indicators Really Tell Us About the Economy
book_thesis: Humans invent indices because reality is too large to hold in the head. A burger, an hour of work, a tube of lipstick or a ship full of grain can turn abstraction into something familiar enough to argue with. That translation is powerful: it can reveal purchasing power, confidence, risk, fragility and manipulation faster than official language can. But a vivid proxy is also dangerous. Some strange measures are grounded and useful; others survive because they are funny, flattering or convenient. This book is about learning to enjoy the strange measures without being fooled by them.

reader_experience.after_20_pages: The reader should feel that economics has become less remote: a burger, a wage-hour and a small consumer object can suddenly carry serious explanatory weight.
reader_experience.after_finishing: The reader should understand why proxies and indices work, why some fail, and how to judge a strange measure before repeating it.
reader_experience.tell_someone: The book should give readers portable stories: the kind of odd comparison they immediately want to explain at dinner.

recommended_opening.reason: It is familiar, commercial, globally recognizable and naturally introduces both usefulness and limitation without starting with methodology.

chapters.central_question: Why can a burger explain exchange rates better than an abstract formula can hold reader attention?
chapters.reader_learns: A familiar object can become a rough translation layer for purchasing power and price-level comparison.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: The Big Mac is useful because it is vivid, not because it is a complete currency model.
chapters.opening_hook: A burger becomes a currency argument.
chapters.ending_transition: If a burger helps, time can help even more.
chapters.visual_opportunity: World map or simple price comparison graphic; must be rights-safe and source-backed.

chapters.central_question: Why does work-time often explain affordability better than converted prices?
chapters.reader_learns: Price becomes meaningful when translated into labor, wages, rent and daily tradeoffs.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: Work-time comparisons feel human, but methodology depends heavily on wage assumptions and local context.
chapters.opening_hook: The same phone costs a few days of work in one city and weeks in another.
chapters.ending_transition: Once numbers become personal, folklore is not far behind.
chapters.visual_opportunity: Work-hours ladder or compact affordability scale.

chapters.central_question: Why do lipstick, underwear and hemlines survive as economic stories even when the evidence is thin?
chapters.reader_learns: A measure can be memorable, narratively satisfying and weakly evidenced at the same time.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: These indicators are commercially irresistible but often contested or folklore.
chapters.opening_hook: A recession supposedly appears first in the bathroom cabinet or underwear drawer.
chapters.ending_transition: Some signals are not folklore; they move through ports and oceans.

chapters.central_question: What can physical movement reveal that consumer anecdotes cannot?
chapters.reader_learns: The physical economy has its own signals: ships, containers, energy and capacity.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: Grounded signals are still not universal explanations; each measures a specific slice.
chapters.opening_hook: Before a product reaches a shelf, a ship or container price may already tell a story.
chapters.ending_transition: Some measures become most powerful when they translate risk rather than money.

chapters.central_question: Can a cigarette-equivalent make pollution understandable without becoming medically misleading?
chapters.reader_learns: Equivalence can make invisible risk legible, but the analogy must not pretend to be literal.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: The story is powerful precisely because it is vivid; that is also why it needs careful limits.
chapters.opening_hook: A city’s air becomes a number of cigarettes.
chapters.ending_transition: Once measures become memorable, they become targets.

chapters.central_question: What happens when people optimize, manipulate or govern by the measure?
chapters.reader_learns: Measures are not passive mirrors; they can change behavior and invite gaming.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: A useful measure can decay when incentives attach to it.
chapters.opening_hook: A number people trust becomes a number people learn to game.
chapters.ending_transition: The same problem now appears in the machine age.

chapters.central_question: Why do AI benchmarks repeat the same old index problem in a new technological costume?
chapters.reader_learns: Benchmarks are indices too: useful, seductive, incomplete and vulnerable to target-chasing.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: The newest measures inherit old problems of scope, incentives and interpretation.
chapters.opening_hook: A model climbs a leaderboard, and everyone argues what the climb means.
chapters.ending_transition: The final question is how to read any weird index without being fooled.
chapters.visual_opportunity: Leaderboard as index metaphor; avoid AI-generated decorative imagery.

chapters.working_title: How to Read a Weird Index
chapters.central_question: How can readers enjoy strange measures while keeping their skepticism intact?
chapters.reader_learns: A useful weird index needs a clear object, source, method, scope, update cadence, limit and incentive check.
chapters.measure_myth_tension: The best strange measures are not perfect; they are honest about what they simplify.
chapters.opening_hook: A good index should make reality readable, not replace reality.

EXCLUDE: AI governance material disconnected from the index promise
unverified internet folklore presented as fact
